say.text: Welcome to class 13. Last time we met people with fire, tools and art. Today we follow them as they walk, and sail, across the planet.

show.text: People Spread Across the Planet

say.text: A migration is a group of people moving to live somewhere new. Our goal today: see how people reached every continent except Antarctica.

show.text: Migration

say.text: It starts in Africa. Our species, Homo sapiens, evolved there about 300,000 years ago.

show.text: 300,000 years ago

say.text: We were not the first to leave. Earlier human species spread out from about 1.8 million years ago, and the ancestors of Neanderthals left before us.

show.text: Earlier species: left Africa from about 1.8 million years ago | Homo sapiens: left much later

ask.q: Who was first to leave Africa?
ask.right: Earlier human species, long before Homo sapiens
wrong: Nobody left, because people evolved on every continent
Neanderthals, after Homo sapiens had left
ask.why: Early humans began spreading into other parts of the world by about 1.8 million years ago, and Neanderthal ancestors left Africa before our species did.

say.text: Now our own species. Some Homo sapiens left early. Bones from caves at Qafzeh and Skhul, in Israel, are about 90,000 to 100,000 years old.

show.text: A cave entrance in Israel, with a modern human skull resting in the dirt

say.text: But DNA from people alive today points to a main wave out of Africa about 50,000 to 60,000 years ago. That group went on to reach every habitable place.

show.text: Fossils: some left 90,000+ years ago | DNA: main wave 50,000 to 60,000 years ago

ask.q: What do the early Israel bones and the DNA tell us together?
ask.right: Some people left early, and a main wave later spread across the world
wrong: Nobody left Africa until 5,000 years ago
Everyone left Africa on the same day
The Israel bones are from Neanderthals, so there is nothing to explain
ask.why: Researchers now think there were several waves out of Africa. Some early groups faded out, and the later wave is the one that spread widely.

say.text: How did people cross the deserts? Wetter spells turned parts of North Africa and Arabia green. People followed the animals they hunted along these corridors.

show.text: Green corridors across North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and the eastern Mediterranean

ask.right: Wet spells that turned desert routes green
wrong: A new continent rising from the sea
ask.why: Climate models show green corridors opened as the climate cycled, and people moved along them following game animals.

say.text: On the way, Homo sapiens met cousins: Neanderthals and Denisovans. DNA shows a small amount of mixing between us and them.

show.text: Neanderthals and Denisovans: small amounts of shared DNA

say.text: Now a big idea that explains almost everything else today. In an ice age, huge amounts of water freeze into ice sheets on land. So the sea level falls.

show.text: Ice age: water locked in ice, sea level falls

say.text: At the coldest time, about 26,000 to 20,000 years ago, the sea was roughly 120 to 130 metres lower than today. Shallow seafloors became dry land, and land bridges appeared.

show.text: 120 to 130 metres lower

ask.q: Why was the sea lower during the ice age?
ask.right: A lot of water was frozen in ice sheets on land
wrong: The land under the sea sank
ask.why: The great ice sheets stored a vast volume of water on land, which lowered global sea level.

say.text: Here is the first result. Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania were joined as one big landmass called Sahul, until seas rose about 10,000 years ago.

show.text: One large landmass, Sahul, joining Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania, with a wider coastline than today

say.text: Even so, Sahul could not be reached on foot. People had to cross open sea from Sunda, the land to its west. The first Australians probably went that way.

show.text: An arrow from Southeast Asia (Sunda) across open water to Sahul

say.text: The best evidence is Madjedbebe, a rock shelter in northern Australia. Dating of the sand around stone tools says people were there about 65,000 years ago.

show.text: A sandstone rock shelter in northern Australia, with stone tools in the soil layers

say.text: Those first tools were not crude. They included grinding stones, ground ochre, and stone hatchets with ground edges.

show.text: Grinding stones | Ground ochre | Ground-edge hatchet heads

ask.right: A rock shelter in northern Australia with signs of people about 65,000 years ago
wrong: A land bridge between Asia and Alaska
ask.why: Madjedbebe is a rock shelter where optical dating of sediment put human occupation at around 65,000 years ago.

say.text: Not everyone agrees on 65,000. Some DNA studies say no earlier than about 55,000 years. A 2025 DNA study says about 60,000. The debate is not over.

show.text: Rock shelter dating: about 65,000 | DNA studies: about 55,000 to 60,000

say.text: Now Europe. At Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, Homo sapiens bones are about 45,000 years old. Neanderthals were gone by about 40,000 years ago.

show.text: About 45,000 years ago: sapiens at Bacho Kiro Cave | About 40,000 years ago: Neanderthals gone

ask.q: Roughly when do the Bulgarian cave bones put Homo sapiens in Europe?
ask.why: The bones from Bacho Kiro Cave are directly dated to about 45,000 years ago, so our species and Neanderthals overlapped in Europe.

say.text: These travellers made art. In Indonesia, a cave painting of human-like figures and a pig is at least 51,200 years old. It is the oldest known picture story.

show.text: Red paint on a cave ceiling: three small human-like figures around a large wild pig

say.text: Now the Americas. In the ice age, sea level fell so far that dry land called Beringia joined Asia and North America.

show.text: Beringia: a wide plain of dry land between Siberia and Alaska at the time of lowest sea level

say.text: For a long time the standard story said people crossed Beringia, then walked south through a gap between ice sheets. That gap is the ice-free corridor. The people were called Clovis.

show.text: An arrow from Beringia south through a narrow gap between two ice sheets

say.text: That story ran into trouble. Monte Verde, in Chile, is about 14,500 years old. And studies suggest the corridor opened after the earliest accepted sites.

show.text: About 14,500 years ago: Monte Verde, Chile | Corridor opens later

ask.q: Why did the 'Clovis first, through the corridor' story fail?
ask.right: Sites in Chile look older than the time the corridor opened
wrong: No one has ever found a Clovis tool
People can't walk between ice sheets
ask.why: Monte Verde is about 14,500 years old, and the corridor appears to have opened later than the earliest accepted sites, so it could not have been the first route.

say.text: A newer idea is the coastal route, the 'kelp highway'. People moved by boat and along the shore of the Pacific, where kelp forests gave fish, shellfish and sea mammals.

show.text: An arrow from Siberia along the Pacific coast, past kelp forests, down to South America

say.text: Proof is hard to find. When the ice melted, the sea rose and flooded that coast, so some of the traces may now lie underwater.

show.text: Rising seas flooded the coast

ask.right: A coastal route along the Pacific, rich in food from the sea
wrong: A paved road through the ice-free corridor
A bridge built over the Bering Strait
ask.why: The kelp highway idea says early Americans followed Pacific shorelines, where kelp forests supported food from the sea.

say.text: Then came footprints at White Sands, New Mexico. Dating of seeds, pollen and mud puts them at 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, about 10,000 years earlier than many once thought.

show.text: Human footprints pressed into pale clay at a dried lake edge

say.text: Many experts are still careful. The dates are backed by dozens of tests, but some critics note the lack of tools or settlements at the spot.

show.text: Supporters: 55 consistent radiocarbon dates | Critics: no tools or settlements found

ask.q: What is true of the White Sands footprint dates?
ask.right: Many tests back them, but some scientists still dispute them
wrong: Everyone agrees they are 5,000 years old
ask.why: Several research groups got matching dates, yet critics still question the dating methods and point out the lack of tools nearby.

say.text: As the ice age ended, seas rose. Before about 13,000 years ago Beringia was dry land. After that it shrank until the land link was gone.

show.text: Before 13,000 years ago: Beringia dry | Later: seas rise and the link is lost

say.text: A mystery now. Megafauna are very big animals, over about 44 kilograms. Huge numbers of them died out in the last 50,000 years.

show.text: Megafauna: animals over about 44 kg

say.text: In Australia, the losses included giant birds, marsupials and reptiles. And if the 65,000-year date holds, people lived beside them for about 20,000 years first.

show.text: Giant birds, marsupials and reptiles

say.text: There are two main suspects: people, by hunting or changing habitats, and climate change. Some scientists blame both together.

show.text: People: hunting, habitat change | Climate: shifts in weather and plants | Or both

ask.q: What are the main suspects in the megafauna extinctions?
ask.right: Human activity, climate change, or a mix of both
ask.why: Researchers have long debated whether climate, human hunting and habitat change, or a combination caused the extinctions.

say.text: A 2025 review counted the papers. 82 name humans as the main cause, 82 name climate, and 71 name a mix. The experts are split.

show.text: Main cause named in extinction papers

say.text: On islands such as Madagascar and New Zealand, there is broad agreement that people played a central role.

show.text: Islands: broad agreement on human impact

say.text: New Zealand was among the last big lands settled. People arrived in double-hulled canoes from East Polynesia, about 1250 to 1300 CE.

show.text: Double-hulled canoes sailing from East Polynesia south-west to New Zealand

ask.q: Roughly when did people settle New Zealand?
ask.why: New Zealand was one of the last habitable lands settled, around 1250 to 1300 CE, by voyagers from East Polynesia.

say.text: That leaves Antarctica. It has no native people. The continent was first sighted in 1820, and there is no record of anyone visiting it before the 1800s.

show.text: The southern polar continent, ringed by ice, with a note: first sighted 1820

ask.q: Which continent has never had a native population?
ask.why: Antarctica has no indigenous people. It was first sighted in 1820, and the only people there now work at research stations.

say.text: Here is the whole journey in one chart: the earliest evidence in each region, in thousands of years ago. Each place came later. Australia and the Americas are still debated.

show.text: Earliest evidence of people, thousands of years ago

say.text: To sum up: people left Africa in waves, crossed seas to Sahul, entered Europe and the Americas by routes we still argue about, and reached Antarctica last of all. Next class: farming.

show.text: 300,000 years ago: sapiens in Africa | About 65,000: Australia (debated) | About 45,000: Europe | 21,000 to 23,000: White Sands (debated) | About 14,500: Chile | 1250 to 1300 CE: New Zealand | 1820: Antarctica sighted

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: People settle northern Australia, if the Madjedbebe date is right. At that time more archaic human groups still lived in Southeast Asia and Australasia, and Neanderthals were still in Europe.
Artists in Sulawesi, Indonesia, paint the oldest known picture story: human-like figures and a pig.
Homo sapiens are in a Bulgarian cave, Neanderthals still live in Europe, and a Sulawesi artist paints a life-size warty pig, dated to about 45,500 years ago.
The coldest stretch of the last ice age. Sea level is far lower, Beringia is dry land, and people leave footprints at White Sands, New Mexico.
People live at Monte Verde, Chile, while the ice sheets are still melting.
The Pleistocene epoch ends. As glaciers melt and seas rise, Beringia shrinks until the land link is gone.
Voyagers from East Polynesia settle New Zealand. Antarctica is still unknown to humans.
Antarctica is first sighted. It is not clear whether Russian, British or American sailors saw it first.

other_side.claim: Homo sapiens left Africa in one main wave about 50,000 to 60,000 years ago.
other_side.other_view: Some fossils suggest earlier trips: the Qafzeh bones in Israel are about 90,000 to 100,000 years old, and a skull fragment at Apidima, Greece, may be over 200,000 years old. A climate-based model suggests several waves, with the earliest groups fading out. Many of these early finds are disputed.

other_side.claim: People first reached Australia about 65,000 years ago.
other_side.other_view: Madjedbebe supports 65,000 years. But one anthropologist argues from DNA that the first arrivals came no earlier than about 55,000 years ago, and most Australian sites date to 43,000 to 54,000 years ago. A 2025 DNA study says about 60,000, and some experts say the debate is not over.

other_side.claim: The White Sands footprints show people in North America 21,000 to 23,000 years ago.
other_side.other_view: Many tests back the dates, but critics say the dating methods may be unreliable and note the lack of tools or settlements at the site. The traditional estimate is 14,000 to 16,000 years ago. Some people also argue that these estimates ignore Indigenous knowledge that people lived in the Americas far longer.

other_side.claim: The first Americans went along the Pacific coast, not through the ice-free corridor.
other_side.other_view: The coastal route is now widely favoured, but it is hard to prove because rising seas flooded the old coast. The corridor was long the standard story, and some think later groups could have used it.

Some studies blame people. One Australian study points to hunting, and a global genetic study ties population declines to the spread of Homo sapiens. Others argue climate was the main driver in Australia, or that North American declines follow climate rather than human numbers. Others find mixed causes by species and region. A 2025 review found the literature split almost evenly.

other_side.claim: The last big Pacific islands were settled between 1200 and 1300 CE.
other_side.other_view: Te Ara places the last Pacific migrations to Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand in 1200 to 1300 CE. Britannica says Hawaii may have been reached as early as 400 CE. Dates for these islands vary with the evidence used.
